p: Fair enough.
Great, thank you, Council Member Felder. Uh, Council Member Brewer followed by Council Member Ressler.

I wish I had Simcha Felder's sense of humor. I do wanna thank Central Park Precinct 24 and 20– Simcha. Those three I want to thank. Retail theft is an issue. In one situation, the Duane Reade put in full-time security and they have zero theft. But the nearby Duane Reade is now– still overwhelmed with security problems because they don't have one and then thefts. I didn't

know how much time or effort or money you put into the idea of retail theft, and if you think the numbers are going down or up.
Retail theft numbers in New York City are going down, like, way down, and it is wonderful to see. It's been happening over the past two years, and Chief LiPetri will tell you all about it.
Thank you.
But specifically Manhattan North.

So as far as retail theft, as the Commissioner said, this year we've seen a 19 percent reduction in retail theft in New York City across all five boroughs. When you look at the five boroughs, geographic boroughs, it's led by Staten Island at 41 percent, followed by Queens at about 21 percent, and Manhattan at about 20 percent. What I'm really proud of is the men and women both on the patrol side and the investigative side when it comes to clearance rate, which means you commit a shoplift and you get arrested. So just four years ago, actually three years ago, that clearance rate was

about 41 percent of the time we made an arrest with a shoplifting complaint. This year it's over 51 percent, and that includes low-level shoplifting crimes. So again, I thank the detectives that have a very high caseload to take on those petty larceny cases. They've done a phenomenal job. We've used the, the tweak in the state law as our friend, meaning, you know, the aggregate amount of merchandise that somebody steals from a particular store, whether it be a CVS on 51st Street or CVS on 55th Street, we're able to aggregate that. And again, it's built off of recidivism. Right.
Okay. I hear you.
And we've done very, very well with that. We still have a lot of work to do, but we're doing well.

Yeah. Okay. Warehouses– so I went to the DCAS warehouse in Queens. It's large. It has lots of extra space. So my question is, how many warehouses does NYPD have? I've been in the cannabis warehouse. There's a lot of cannabis in there. And I just was wondering how many

warehouses you have, what the cost is, can you reduce?
So we're actually actively working right now on, uh, ideally consolidating some of our warehouses, including the warehouse you're referencing.
The cannabis one.
There are other things there as well, but yes, there is—
[interposing] I've been through it.

cannabis at that facility. Unfortunately, we did have funding, in 20— before 2020 to do a full consolidated property clerk, which would have taken care of this. That funding doesn't exist, so we're trying to be creative now and look at properties in some of the outer boroughs where we think we may be able to get out of some of the leases that are problematic.
Can you update us on that? I knew you had a fire in one too in Brooklyn.
Yes.
So can you update us on warehouses? I do believe that around the city all agencies can be consolidating, not just PD, and I think it would save some money.

I think that's a great idea, and we are working closely with DCAS. So I think the best thing would be for us to put together for you an update on what we're doing with DCAS to address the warehouse needs with exactly the goal you're saying, to have it be more state-of-the-art so we don't have issues, and then also to consolidate so that we reduce the footprint.
Thank you. Tow pound, always my question. None in Manhattan. Is that a problem? Are you ever going to find a tow pound in the borough of Manhattan?
It continues to be, unfortunately, the same challenge that we had in–
The same— since past—

It's just since— it's unfortunately just the cost of real estate in Manhattan is really challenging. We've had

a few sites where we thought we might be able to have a somewhat smaller footprint but still have something so that people didn't have to travel quite as far if they were booted or other things like that with their car. Unfortunately, those have fallen through, but we do continue to look with DCAS to see if we can restore a footprint to Manhattan. Okay, just because I had the same question since Cuomo closed Pier 76. That was quite a few years ago. Okay. And then what— NYCHA, the bureau in getting any more money, less money in terms of PSA? That is a really important division of NYPD. The reason I ask is I believe— I love NYCHA, I love the residents. I strongly believe that if we were to focus on NYCHA, not just you, but in a holistic way, you'd have far fewer issues.

So I am very proud to tell you that in NYCHA specifically, New York City is having its safest start to the year on record, with major crime there down 10 percent, murders down 43 percent, shooting incidents down 24 percent, shooting victims down 30 percent, robberies down 24 percent, and burglaries down 19 percent. The crime story in NYCHA this year— or the crime picture in NYCHA this

year is vastly improved from last year. NYCHA and the Bronx are the two places where we are seeing the largest crime reductions, and I give a tremendous—
[interposing] It was the highest to start with though.

I give a tremendous amount of— yes, absolutely. And I give a tremendous amount of credit to the chief of Department and the Chief of Crime Control Strategies on their precision policing, which is focusing additional resources where the violent crime occurs. And sometimes you can set a strategy, put a strategy in place and don't see results. And this one, they put the strategy in place and they are driving real results.
What else is needed for NYCHA?

Oh, we could have a very long conversation about that, but I think in terms of policing resources, you are seeing very good outcomes. There's obviously a lot more work that can be done. I think a lot of it is on the social services side, but from policing at this time, we

feel like we have the right strategy in place and the right resources to deliver results.
All right. Thank you.
Thank you. Council Member Ressler, followed by Councilmember Banks.
Thank you so much, Chair Lee and Chair Feliz. Appreciate both of your leadership. And Commissioner, it's always good to see you.
Good to see you.

I disagree with you on a number of issues, but I appreciate your competence and the integrity that you've returned to the department. And think that a number of things are moving in a positive direction, and I want to credit you for that. I also just wanna take a moment to shout out Chief Obe and her XO Chief O'Sullivan, who have been really responsive to some of the issues that we face in the 84, and I'm really grateful for that. They've made a real effort, and it's been very much appreciated, so I just want to take a moment to say something nice before I give you a hard time.

Troubled by your response to Chair— Council Member Brooks-Powers' comments– questions around incarceration. You know, just to put a finer point on it, we're about three years away from the opening of the Brooklyn jail. We have twice as many people incarcerated in Rikers right now from Brooklyn as what that jail can accommodate. We need an all-hands approach from the Police Department, from the Department of Correction, from the courts, and from a whole lot of other stakeholders including the council, to work together to drive down incarceration in New York City. And I'd hope that you'd be a partner in that effort so that we can reduce unnecessary incarceration, reduce the amount of time that people are incarcerated, all working together as much as possible to achieve the smaller and safer vision of what Close Rikers is about.
Understood.
I was also deeply troubled by the data you shared around BHEARD. So I'll just walk through the data that I think I heard, and you can correct me if I said something–
HOld on. I got to get it out.

You get it out, I'll talk while you get it out. Okay, so 4.3 million calls to 911 annually. You said that in the first 4 months of this year, only 17,961 of the calls you received were appropriate for B-HEARD. Is that right?

Hold on. Yeah, Alex says yes, that is correct. So that's about 54,000 calls annually. So 54,000 calls out of 4.3 million is that 1.2 percent of calls into 911 are appropriate for B-HEARD according to the Police Department's view.
The total number of each— of nonviolent–
[interposing] Totally.

non-weapons calls for emotionally disturbed 2024 was 85,793. So we believe that up— if you say that that's going to be constant every year, or, you know, the percentage is about two percent of 911 calls for service under the current criteria.

I had you at 1.2 based on the first four months of this year. You're saying in 24 it was a little higher, but in that range. So firstly, I just think for this administration that's taking a different approach, that we want to invest in alternative responses for nonviolent situations, saying that one percent to wo percent of our calls is appropriate for B-HEARD, I think is unfortunate. But even more troubling, which is not on your plate, is that for 97 percent of the calls year to date, just 1,411 out of the 17,961 calls that were appropriate for Be Heard according to you, just 2.6 percent of those calls were actually responded to by Be Heard. So what—
[interposing] I have 1,411 out of 17,961.
Oh, so that’s seven percent–
7.9% from January 1st to April 30th.

That’s right. So to put a finer point on all of that, that is 0.01 percent of calls that B-HEARD is responding to. 0.01

percent of calls. That is so small, it's a rounding error, it's negligible. Does the program even exist? We're spending gosh knows how many tens, hundreds of millions of dollars on this program. It was functioning at some point. It doesn't seem like it's even functioning today. So we have some questions for the fire department and health and hospitals for why Be Heard is essentially irrelevant. I think that of the lowest of low-hanging fruit in the vision of what the Office of Community Safety can be and eventually the Department of Community Safety to my colleagues– was that nicely done? Thank you, ma'am. The— there's— we got a co-sponsor in the room. This is the lowest of low-hanging fruit, and it's an embarrassment. Can— well, I'll do round two because I talk too much. Brooklyn Central Booking has been a serious problem. I'm grateful that your team has finally confirmed for us this morning that we'll get a tour. We've seen too many fatalities and serious issues there. And in round two, I'd like to dig in more on response times. So thank you, Chairs.
Thank you. We'll add you to round two. And we— oh no, not yet. And then now we have Council Member Banks. Go ahead.

Thank you, Chair, and good to see you, Commissioner, to your team. Penn Track, the Penn Track, we still have concerns and frustrations around the Penn Track. If we can get an update for the 42nd Council District as to what's going on. And obviously with the warmer weather that is approaching— well, it's here already, Residents constantly complain about the Penn Track. And I know there's been ongoing stuff, operations back there, but it would be a great idea if you kept the community updated as to what was being done. Obviously not the sensitive stuff, but at least let the community know, the progress that is being made, or if any progress is being made, as opposed to continually see the visual we always see, and that's sex workers walking the streets back there. And also, if I— let me finish. The issue, you know, there's been multiple social media videos that have been made about the Penn Track ongoing– and, you know, this has continued to put a blight, or it attempts to put a

blight on the 42nd Council District. But if residents are hearing and, and seeing, PD is working on their behest as far as to try to solve this issue. I think that would go a long way with helping out as far as on the PR side or communicating to the community. So if we can get an update, I greatly appreciate that.
The Chief of Department will answer the question.
Sure. So obviously, Chris, you know, many, many years in East [sic] New York–
[interposing] Yes. Good to see you.

Good to see you. You know, dealing with the the Pennsylvania track, you know, in and around that Linden Boulevard area. You're right, it is stubborn and it is somewhat frustrating in that, you know, with the change in the law and a class action lawsuit that happened years ago, it has hurt our local enforcement, our local enforcement meaning, you know, the precincts aren't really able to deal with the actual prostitution/John situation. But our Vice Enforcement Unit, consistently,

consistently hits the Penn Track, as does our human trafficking team in and around some of those stubborn hotels, motels, 100 Jersey, things of that nature.
Right.
I've also tasked the precinct commander to put a plan in place to deal with low-level crime in and around those hotels along the Penn Track, meaning the quality of life issues that we do see–
[interposing] Right.

that facilitates some of the violence when it comes to, you know, the prostitution. But I will tell you, it is the number one location in the city of New York when it comes to enforcement by our specialty units, namely VICE and the human trafficking side on

I know there was efforts up in Roosevelt also, so if we can get the same type of attention that would definitely— I know it made an impact in that particular district, I believe, from what I've heard. So if we can get that same type of attention, I'll greatly appreciate it.

And the last thing pertaining to the 75th Precinct— You know, I represent close to four commands and therefore the city council, but particularly for the 75th Precinct, it's been a long-held complaint or frustration knowing that the 75th Precinct is probably one of the largest commands throughout the entire city. When will we be able to get an opportunity to split that command? You know, on the southern part of the district, we had a major, major increase in population with the housing that's being built on that side. And I believe it's long time needed for the 75th to be split. I mean, it goes all the way from Starrett [sic] City all the way into Jamaica, up in Sandy's district. The residents want that.
You don't need to tell the Chief of Department that. He is a former CO of the 75.

I know he's a— well, I had a great relationship with him when he was the former– so he understands that. We just need to see action. We need to see something done pertaining to that particular issue, because this goes back over

20, 30 years, the need to have the command split, even if it's some type of satellite that was put on the southern side, like in the Gateway area, it would go a long way.

I'll just answer very, very quickly. Just like the Police Commissioner talks about the Bronx getting the most resources as far as now two patrol boroughs, by far the 75 gets the most resources in all of Brooklyn North, other than some precincts in the Bronx. And again, you know, I had the most, the most RMPs, I had the most cops, I had the most cameras, I had the most Argus cameras. So, pointed, it is a large command with a lot going on.
Right.
But that's why we put, you know– DI Hines there, has a lot of experience being
[interposing] DI Hines is doing a pretty good job.
in East New York, and he's going to do a phenomenal job.
And I will just ask Christine to speak about the process to build a new— to create a new precinct. Go ahead.
Yeah. So, when we look at, you know, we take into account obviously all the factors in the precinct, the crime, the population, everything you mentioned.
Yes.

But there's also obviously the real estate element of it. The most recent newly built precinct, the 116, was $108 million. So right now we don't have funding for a new precinct, but if that were to move forward, we would need those resources and, you know, work.
I'm also happy to continue conversation with you–
[interposing] We look forward to having a sidebar conversation. Thank you.
Thank you.

Thank you. Actually, talking about capital and going into that theme– so looking at the capital plan, it appears to be heavily front-loaded with $432.9 million planned in the current fiscal year, and then it drops to about $16.4 million in FY 29. And we know that capital plans are

generally front-loaded, and there are some large capital projects wrapping up in the next few years. Could you generally explain some of the big projects happening in the next few years that drives some of these changes and also give some context on the planning of projects?

Yes. So part of the reason that it's so front-loaded is, as you mentioned, large projects. So one is, as we mentioned earlier, the infusion of capital funding now for vehicles. So there's a significant amount of funding early in the plan so that we can jumpstart continuing to replace those vehicles. And also our largest single project is also in the early years of the plan, which is Rodman's Neck. So we're working on that, which should be done by the summer of 28. So those are the two biggest things, and then the others are spread out more throughout the plan. What we do when we plan our capital budget, it changes with each financial plan because we take a look at where we are in the construction process–
[interposing] right.
and whether or not we have CPs yet. And obviously with the procurement—
[interposing] The drawings been done, and–

Exactly. So things tend to shift. Certain things we will push out, but then at the same time, OMB works very well with us and they're very flexible. If something's moving more quickly or we have a need earlier than it's reflected in the capital plan, we will look to accelerate those funds.

Okay, perfect. And then for asset forfeiture funding, which I mentioned earlier in the statement– Preliminary Budget response, council called upon NYPD to utilize the asset forfeiture dollars for eligible costs that expand the investigative resources before calling on city tax levy dollars. So how much asset forfeiture has NYPD used over the course of this fiscal year, and what are the costs associated with it?

So right now we have a balance of about $52 million in asset

forfeiture. Of that— and sometimes it's just the timing of how it's drawn down— of that $28 million— apologies, $38 million has already been accounted for, so there's $14 million balance. So I completely understand the perspective of utilize this first instead of using city funds. We work very closely to establish what is eligible for asset forfeiture. There are very strict guidelines on the uses of asset forfeiture. And the things we utilize it for are things that are really critical to the department— use it for lab supplies and equipment. We use it for critical training for our officers and travel to and from that training as well as supplies and equipment and initiatives tied to investigations. So those are the types of things where if we weren't using this money, we would then have to use city funds.
Right.

So most of it is actually already accounted for, and then we'll go forward and replenish those items I just listed. So if not for using it there, we are in fact not just trying to hold it to do something. It's just

supplementing the normal things that we would utilize our city funds for as well.

Right.Okay, perfect. And then, the Deputy Speaker had to leave, but she wanted me to ask this question. Another goal of— going back to the, I think, the racial equity plan. Another goal of NYPD's in the preliminary racial equity plan is to quantify, track, and analyze racial disparities in stops, frisks, and searches in an effort to reduce those disparities. This is listed as a medium-term goal to be completed by 2028. Uh, do you have any data on stop and frisk from data collected from the How Many Stops Act that the council passed?
So with regard to the How Many Stops Act, as part of that law, we put out data with regard to level 1, level 2, and level 3, and level 3 encounters. So that data is put out, I believe it's quarterly.

I have the data. So investigative encounters, 2025 full year, Level 1, $2 million plus. Level 2, $31,159. Level 3, $26,405. For

context perspective, that number was $680,000 in 2011. CHAIRPERSON LEE:: Which one? Level 3?
Yes.
Okay, 680.
So we went from 680,000 Level 3 stops in 2011 to 26,405 Level 3 stops in 2025.
Got it.
And this year, so far, we have about 16 percent less or fewer stops, Level 3 stops.

Okay, across— okay, Level 3. Okay. Okay, and how will the training initiative goals affect this aspect of the department's work, and how will this review inform you of the relevant units and commands for retraining?

Yeah, so we've created something called the Racial Disparities Review Committee. That's something— it's part of the plan. It's also something we're doing with the Monitor, right? So there's actually— it's the

Monitor's— the Monitor team are quite involved and obviously don't want to speak for the Monitor. But what we're doing is we are looking at data, doing that in a very, you know, deliberate way and thoughtful way, working off of a model that the monitors team used and sort of further developing that out ourselves. And in looking at that, you know, to the extent you have outlier commands, we want to understand what's happening. What's driving disparities, and just really in part to understand it, but then, you know, if there are— if there are disparities that we can't account for, making sure we can address them. So we're looking at department-level data, like the department as a whole and trends over time. But then also we want to understand what's happening in any outlier commands.
Okay, great. And then how do you track that data? Is it by borough? Is it by precinct?

So, again, we're sort of developing kind of an internal model, building off of the monitors team's work, and we have both sort of in-house talent, people we've hired to

work on this. We also have some external help as well. And then again, in sort of— that model is still being built out. We're not there yet. This is a very complicated process, right? It's going to play out over time. But in doing that, we're looking at department-level data. We can look— ultimately, we'll be able to look at borough-level, command-level data, as well. We're not— again, but this is very much a process that's going to play out over many months.
Great. Okay. Thank you so much. And I'll pass it to Chair Feliz.

Thank you so much, Chair Lee. A few more questions on overtime, and then we'll move on to other issues. And trust me, I wish I did not have to spend this much time talking about overtime, but obviously a big part of the budget, overtime. To what extent do you think increasing headcount can potentially decrease overtime?

Again, there are trade-offs. So I can't answer that question specifically. It certainly— if we had a larger headcount, it certainly would have— would bring down the overtime budget this summer, for the special

events, meaning we wouldn't have to go to the 12-hour tours. But in other cases, like, it wouldn't make a dent. So for example, if we needed an officer to work 2 extra hours for, you know, in a zone, it— larger headcount wouldn't get rid of it. And oftentimes it said that more headcount, more overtime. I don't necessarily believe that to be true, because I believe if you responsibly manage overtime, you can avoid that.
What would you say are the top three things that need— would have to happen in an ideal world for us to be able to make the dent on the issue of overtime that I think we all want to make?

I think we have made a dent on the issue of overtime. I think the data that I provided earlier, calendar year 2025 overtime down 12.4 percent, fiscal year 2026 the first three quarters overtime down 10 percent, and the fact that the fiscal year '26 overtime spend is projected to be six percent lower than the historical average going back to 2016, if you put it in today's dollars and if you exclude the transit program that the the governor

is funding. When we think about overtime, yes, the numbers go up, and that's because the cops rightfully get paid more. And so that increases overtime spend.
All right, moving on to school safety agents and school crossing guards. Can you give us the new budgeted headcount for school safety agents and crossing guards?

Yes, I can. Okay. School safety agents were cut by 264 positions to 3,651. Does someone have school crossing guards in front of them? If not, I can get it here. Yes. Hold on, I have it. I have it. Do you have it? School— I don't see it here.
So we just recently hired 94 in May, so that leaves us with 31 vacancies. The allocated budget is $2,309.
Kristine, do you have the specific numbers for school safety agents? Sorry, sorry, for school crossing guards.
So I have 2,309 for the allocation. We just hired a class of 94 in May, so that leaves us with 31 vacancies.
Thank you, Chief.
All right. Can you tell us how the current headcount compares to the headcount for the last five years for school safety agents and school crossing guards?
Down, but we will get you those specific numbers. Do you— I don't have it by year here. I just have this year.
And I know we're reducing the school safety agents by 264. Do you think what we have right now is enough?
No.
If not, why the cut?

I was disappointed about that cut, although I understood it because those were vacant positions. My hope had been to hire up to our previous authorized headcount, and we were looking at a number of different ways to gin interest in taking that test and to have basically more people interested in becoming school safety agents. And the reason we didn't— we weren't up to headcount is because we didn't have enough, “qualified” candidates. So we were looking at a number of factors, including looking at some of the physical

requirements to become school safety agents, which seemed to be, to my mind, out of line with what the job requires. So I was hoping to make progress increasing the number of school safety agents before this cut occurred. But I do understand that it occurred because those positions were vacant at the time.

All right. Moving on to ghost cars. So as we know, there's a lot of different agencies that are involved when it comes to enforcing rules related to ghost cars, fake paper plates, and etcetera. And I know there's been some changes. The sanitation department is playing a bigger role. Can you talk to us about the different agencies and the different processes and roles that each play, including the NYPD?

Sure. The Sanitation Department addresses vehicles that are derelict. So they are below some certain dollar value, some dollar value, and the sanitation depa— and they're just sitting on the streets, and the Sanitation Department has the authority to get rid of them themselves. The Police Department has a lot going on with ghost cars

and non-derelict vehicles, and Chief Obe can talk to you about some of our enforcement there.

Okay. So, with ghost car— ghost plate operations, it's an interagency ghost– interagency initiative. So it's not just done in a, you know, silo, just NYPD. We work very closely with our law enforcement partners, typically along bridges and tunnels. So New York State Police, MTA, the NYPD, PAPD. Year to date, we've had about 19 joint operations, and resulting in 291 arrests, 12,000+ summons issued, and 1,278 vehicles seized. In your district, I know that there were some concerns. You know, that work continues along Fordham Road and some of the locations that you gave us. I don't have that specifically. I'll get back to you on that. But the work we do is totally separate from what Sanitation does. We work along bridges and tunnels, and it's a multiagency effort.

Right. Yeah. So about two years ago, a while back, had a hearing on the issue of ghost cars. And we were told that the NYPD didn't have enough space to tow or to be able to properly enforce the rule on the issue of ghost cars.

Is that still the case? I know you've been working on getting new towing space.

So it's totally separate. I know that's what a council member always talks about, but this is totally separate. So as a result of the multi-agency efforts that we have with the other law enforcement agencies, the storage is not an issue for us at all because we tap into the MTA and the TBTA. They have ample space when it comes to storage, so we don't suffer from that problem, separate from that other type of work.

Okay, good. All right, drones. So, as I mentioned in my opening statement, saw a fascinating video yesterday. Individuals in the Bronx had engaged in gun violence. The local precinct used the drone to basically make sure that they were able to– to make sure they were apprehended quickly. And we're thankful for those officers who were running towards two individuals who had just engaged in gun violence and also still had loaded weapons. So, curious, and I know if you can't share this information for public safety-related reasons, all fine, understood. But can you talk to us about the

use of drones? Does every precinct have one, or is it some of the cars?

So the Chief of Department is going to answer a lot of the specifics to your question, and our use of drones is amazing. I would just like to say upfront that I would like to expand the Department's use of drones. We do not have drones at every precinct, and I believe we should have drones at every precinct. As the drone management in the city is currently set up, the funding and the overall, like, management of drone expansion is currently at the Department of Information Technology and Telecommunications. And I believe, given that the NYPD is the biggest user of drones and there are such incredible opportunities to use this to— that technology to drive public safety, that we should be in control of our own destiny in terms of expanding our drone program. But the chief will tell you about how great it is.

Sure. So obviously I'm not going to get into specific precincts on where our drones are being launched. So we have three areas in Brooklyn, one area in the Bronx, and one area in

northern Manhattan. Each contains two docks which can obviously fly two drones. So the drone can only go out for a specific amount of time, comes back, and we put up the second drone. We've done approximately 5,000 flights this year alone, about 4,000 of those 5,000 are drones as first responders. Our response time when we put up a drone to the actual 911 call is less than three minutes. It's about 2.5 minutes. The success stories that you're talking about, I can specifically talk about the one you're talking about on May 24th, when yes, there was a response to a shots fired, and yes, we did grab two different individuals with pistols. So it's highly successful. I agree with the Police Commissioner. We're looking to obviously explore and expand our drones. In addition to the 4,000 first responder flights that we've done this year, there's another 1,000 that we used for either missing, you know, beach drone activity, parades, things of that nature. So we are up and running, and it has been a great tool for us so far.

Chair, I apologize. I just found the information you were looking for on

school crossing guards. I just want to make sure that it's in line with what the Chief had previously said. So as of May 13th, we employ 2,290 school crossing guards, including 2,211 level one’s and 79 level two’s. The budgeted headcount for school crossing guards is 2,309, which breaks out to 2,219 level one’s and 90 level two’s.

All right, thank you for that data. Just curious on the issue of technology and drones, in what cases do we use drones? They're more effective for many reasons. They're cheaper, which means you could purchase more. They're faster. If you have more, you could have them in different locations. In what cases do we use drones versus helicopters? I'm sure every New Yorker has heard those helicopters when there's a serious incident?

So, look, you know, we obviously know the price difference, right, between the fuel and things of that nature. I will say this, when we can put up a drone, that drone's going up. You know, there are restrictions, and also the infrastructure sometimes— or I should say, you know,

tight locations, things of that nature. Yeah, we're able to use that drone in between buildings. You know, our emergency service unit uses it tactically for barricaded perpetrators. And, you know, we have approximately 80 drones, and I'm telling you, we use it as much as we can.

Good. The Executive Plan included $6.5 million for drone-based grant. How do you plan on utilizing this funding? And also, can you talk to us about the new developments? I know you've been working with the federal government to have more authority to be able to take down drones, which is—

Yes, we got $6.5 million from the federal government to use to buy drone mitigation equipment. We have spent that money and purchased the equipment. We also have members of our counterterrorism team trained on using that equipment and trained with the FBI specifically on drone mitigation. So, for the first time at the World Cup this year and events in New York City surrounding the World Cup, the NYPD will be working directly with our federal partners, with our own equipment and our

own personnel on drone mitigation. And I will say that is a very important first step. As for doing it beyond the World Cup, beyond that special event, it is still hazy, and I am not at this time certain how it will work.
